newsitem.title: ITALY: Turkish President says Kurdish autonomy groundless.
newsitem.headline: Turkish President says Kurdish autonomy groundless.

text.p: Turkish President Suleyman Demirel on Wednesday dismissed calls for Kurdish autonomy and accused what he called "terrorist" groups of trying to force the creation of a Kurdish state.
"We cannot talk of a Kurdish aspiration to freedom since the Kurds are full Turkish citizens," Demirel told reporters in Venice during a visit to Italy.
"There is no reason for a demand for freedom because there is no motivation," he added.
More than 20,000 people have been killed in a 12-year conflict between government and PKK guerrillas fighting for autonomy or independence in the mainly Kurdish southeast.

"In Turkey there are also innocent victims," Demirel said. "Four thousand people of the forces of order have been killed by real assassins, but you never hear about them, you only hear about these aspirations for liberty."
Turkish authorities said on Tuesday that its security forces killed 118 Kurdish guerillas in clashes that spilled over the mountainous border into northern Iraq.
They said 11 members of security forces had also died in fighting with Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK) rebels.
"There are pressure and lobby groups working in Europe against Turkey, a democratic, safe, liberal, free country," he told reporters. He did not go into details.
"The aim of the terrorists is to divide the country and violate the territorial integrity of Turkey and thus create a Kurdish state."
He urged Europe to understand the problem his country faced. "Citizens of the Turkish republic, whatever their origins, have lived together for more than a thousand years," he said.
"If terrorism is accepted, it will be considered as something based on justifiable motives. This will lead to enormous bloodshed in the world."
Deputy Prime Minister told Demirel on Tuesday that Italy was worried about Turkey's human rights record and hoped it would improve given the country's desire to join the European Union.
Many allegations of human rights abuses come from the mainly-Kurdish southeast of Turkey where 10 provinces are under emergency rule.
